# The Mercy of Unfinished Things

On the desk beside me is a notebook with three pages left blank. I have owned it for six years. Its early pages contain train times for journeys I no longer remember taking, a recipe for soup I never cooked, and the opening line of a story about a woman who finds a seashell in her coat pocket. After that line, nothing. For years, those blank pages faintly accused me. They seemed less like paper than like a small, patient tribunal. Then, one winter afternoon, I opened the notebook and felt something unexpected: relief. There was still room.

We live under a quiet cult of completion. Finish your plate, your degree, your novel, your inbox. Close the loop. Clear the deck. Even rest is often assigned a purpose: sleep so you can perform tomorrow, walk so you can return with an idea. Against this, the unfinished thing looks lazy or embarrassed, a guest who has stayed too long. Yet a life made only of completions would be airless. Every door would be shut. Every question would have become an answer, and every answer would be standing in the corner with its arms folded.

Look closely at anything finished and you will find the ghosts of its earlier attempts. The chair carries the memory of joints that did not hold. The symphony contains, by exclusion, melodies no audience will hear. A loaf of bread is the edible survivor of collapsed dough, scorched crusts, and afternoons when the kitchen smelled of disappointment. Skill is not the absence of these failures but a growing friendship with them. The expert is often simply someone who has remained willing to be a beginner in private, repeatedly, after the nobility of beginning has worn off.

Unfinished things also make time porous. A half-knitted scarf waits with its needles crossed like an unfinished sentence. Someone will return to it with different hands: older, perhaps steadier, perhaps finally willing to admit that the pattern was too difficult. A pencil mark on a wall recording a child’s height is complete only until the next birthday. Even a garden, which appears to be the very emblem of patient accomplishment, is mostly an agreement to continue. No gardener stands back in August and says, with total sincerity, “There. Nature is done.” A completely finished garden would only be a photograph, admirable, silent, and quietly unable to survive another season.

None of this means abandonment deserves a laurel wreath. Some unfinished matters ache because they should be finished. The apology postponed until pride has hardened. The message to a sick friend, drafted and redrafted while the right words become less important than the arriving ones. The loose stair, the unpaid debt, the conversation everyone in the house can hear not happening. There are silences that protect possibility, and silences that merely pass injury from one day to the next. Wisdom begins in telling them apart, which is rarely as easy as making a list.

Perhaps the test is whether the unfinished thing still has a pulse. Does it change when you return to it? Does it ask something of you beyond punishment? A living project can tolerate neglect for a season and then suddenly open, like a cupboard whose sticking door gives way. A dead one keeps demanding the same ceremonial guilt. You are allowed to bury those. You are allowed to decide that the person who wanted to learn the violin, restore the boat, or read the enormous Russian novel was not mistaken, exactly, but was making a proposal you are free to decline.

This gentleness matters most with people, because people are not projects, though we often treat them as such. We ask friends to become consistent, partners to become legible, parents to become the simple figures our childhood required. We narrate them in completed sentences. She always does this. He will never understand. Then someone surprises us, and instead of welcoming the surprise, we feel briefly inconvenienced, as if a character has disobeyed the plot. To love anyone is to consent to revisions. The person before you is not the final proof of the person you remember.

Grief makes this especially plain. After a death, the world fills with conversations that cannot be concluded and questions that seem to have been waiting for precisely the wrong moment. What was the name of that neighbor? Why did you leave the city? Were you happy in the yellow house? The cruelty is not only that no answer comes, but that new questions keep arriving. Yet love does not become unreal because its object is beyond reach. It changes tense. It becomes an unfinished thing we carry carefully, without demanding that care turn it into something else.

There is a larger incompleteness beneath all these small ones. None of us will be present for the final edit. The email will outlive its urgency; the list of errands will outlast the afternoon, and perhaps much more. This can sound bleak, but it also releases us from a foolish contract. We were never required to finish existence before being allowed to inhabit it. We can wash one cup without solving the kitchen. We can begin the letter without knowing its ending. We can spend an hour so completely that, for a while, it needs no consequence at all.

The notebook remains on my desk. Sometimes I use its last pages; sometimes I leave them alone. Their emptiness no longer looks like a verdict. It looks like weather held in reserve, or three unlit rooms in a house where someone is still awake. Tonight I may copy out the old sentence about the woman and the seashell. I may discover that she has just come from a beach, or a funeral, or the coat pocket of someone she loved. Then again, I may simply close the cover. A beginning does not always need to be kept. Sometimes it is enough that, after all these years, it can still be made.

P1 (~116):
"On the desk beside me is a notebook with three pages left blank. I have owned it for six years. Its early pages contain train times for journeys I no longer remember taking, a recipe for soup I never cooked, and the opening line of a story about a woman who finds a sea shell in her coat pocket. After that line, nothing. For years, those blank pages faintly accused me. They seemed less like paper than like a small, patient tribunal. Then, one winter afternoon, I opened the notebook and felt something unexpected: relief. There was still room."
Count 112? Fine.

P2:
"I live under a quiet cult of completion. Finish your plate, your degree, your novel, your inbox. Close the loop. Clear the deck. Even rest is often assigned a purpose: sleep so you can perform tomorrow, walk so you can return with an idea. Against this, the unfinished thing looks lazy or embarrassed, a guest who has stayed too long. Yet a life made only of completions would be airless. Every door would be shut. Every question would have become an answer, and every answer would be standing in the corner with its arms folded."
~98.

P3:
"Look closely at anything finished and you will find the ghosts of its earlier attempts. The chair carries the memory of joints that did not hold. The symphony contains, by exclusion, melodies no audience will hear. A loaf of bread is the edible survivor of collapsed dough, scorched crusts, and afternoons when the kitchen smelled of disappointment. Skill is not the absence of these failures but a growing friendship with them. The expert is often simply someone who has remained willing to be a beginner in private, repeatedly, after the nobility of beginning has worn off."
~99.

P4:
"Unfinished things also make time porous. A half-knitted scarf waits with its needles crossed like an unfinished sentence. Someone will return to it with different hands: older, perhaps steadier, perhaps finally willing to admit that the pattern was too difficult. A pencil mark on a wall recording a child's height is complete only until the next birthday. Even a garden, which appears to be the very emblem of patient accomplishment, is mostly an agreement to continue. No gardener stands back in August and says, with total sincerity, 'There. Nature is done.'"
~99.

P5:
"None of this means abandonment deserves a laurel wreath. Some unfinished matters ache because they should be finished. The apology postponed until pride has hardened. The message to a sick friend, drafted and redrafted while the right words become less important than the arriving ones. The loose stair, the unpaid debt, the conversation everyone in the house can hear not happening. There are silences that protect possibility, and silences that merely pass injury from one day to the next. Wisdom begins in telling them apart, which is rarely as easy as making a list."
~100.

P6:
"Perhaps the test is whether the unfinished thing still has a pulse. Does it change when you return to it? Does it ask something of you beyond punishment? A living project can tolerate neglect for a season and then suddenly open, like a cupboard whose sticking door gives way. A dead one keeps demanding the same ceremonial guilt. You are allowed to bury those. You are allowed to decide that the person who wanted to learn the violin, restore the boat, or read the enormous Russian novel was not mistaken, exactly, but was making a proposal you are free to decline."
~101.

P7:
"This gentleness matters most with people, because people are not projects, though I often treat them as such. I ask friends to become consistent, partners to become legible, parents to become the simple figures my childhood required. I narrate them in completed sentences. She always does this. He will never understand. Then someone surprises me, and instead of welcoming the surprise, I feel briefly inconvenienced, as if a character has disobeyed the plot. To love anyone is to consent to revisions. The person before you is not the final proof of the person you remember."
~101.

P8:
"Grief makes this especially plain. After a death, the world fills with conversations that cannot be concluded and questions that seem to have been waiting for precisely the wrong moment. What was the name of that neighbor? Why did you leave the city? Were you happy in the yellow house? The cruelty is not only that no answer comes, but that new questions keep arriving. Yet love does not become unreal because its object is beyond reach. It changes tense. It becomes an unfinished thing I carry carefully, without demanding that care turn it into something else."
~103.

P9:
"There is a larger incompleteness beneath all these small ones. None of us will be present for the final edit. The email will outlive its urgency; the list of errands will outlast the afternoon, and perhaps much more. This can sound bleak, but it also releases me from a foolish contract. I was never required to finish existence before being allowed to inhabit it. I can wash one cup without solving the kitchen. I can begin the letter without knowing its ending. I can spend an hour so completely that, for a while, it needs no consequence at all."
~103.

P10:
"The notebook remains on my desk. Sometimes I use its last pages; sometimes I leave them alone. Their emptiness no longer looks like a verdict. It looks like weather held in reserve, or three unlit rooms in a house where someone is still awake. Tonight I may copy out the old sentence about the woman and the seashell. I may discover that she has just come from a beach, or a funeral, or the coat pocket of someone she loved. Then again, I may simply close the cover. A beginning does not always need to be kept. Sometimes it is enough that, after all these years, it can still be made."
~113.
